latin.318: Non est autem verbum dicitur in hac interrogatione accipiendum relative ad solam Scripturam, ut facit vir doctus, sed relative ad Scripturam & omnes Theologos, qui nunquam dixerunt Adamum esse peccatum nostrum, aut iniustitiam nostram, aut nos esse iniustitiam in Adamo. Diversitas enim phrasium cum de Christo & Adamo agitur in negotio justificationis & condemnationis arguit inter utrumque diversitatem atque disparitatem. Itaque nos quidem decet iis phrasibus esse contentos, quae in Scriptura occurrunt, & vero nos iis admodum contenti sumus, sed decet nos tamen eas phrases attente considerare, rationes expendere, quare sic vel sic Deus mentem suam expressit, vel non expressit; in quo nobis suo exemplo praeiverunt Apostoli, ipsum etiam Scripturae silentium interdum urgentes. Nullae autem sunt apud Apostolum locutiones quae imputationem immediatam manifeste designent, immo ne obscure quidem quae designent, visae sunt.
latin.319: GAR. 2. Locis illis, ubi dicitur Christus justitia nostra, nulla inter Adamum & Christum instituitur comparatio: quae si instituta fuisset, ut factum est Roman. 5. quis nescit annon ea phrasi usurus fuerit Paulus, qua doceret Adamum esse peccatum nostrum, sicut Christus est justitia nostra, etsi non eadem omnino ratione. PLAC. Ego vero inde argumentor, quod ubi nullam instituit Apostolus comparationem Christi inter & Adamum usurpat illam de Christo locutionem, ubi autem aliquam inter utrumque instituit comparationem ab ea abstinet. Quanquam, ut dixi, non ad solam Scripturam, sed etiam ad Theologos omnes habetur respectus, qui locutionem illam nunquam usurpant de Adamo.
latin.320: GAR. 3. Probabilis tamen ratio reddi potest, quare Adam non dicatur peccatum nostrum, sicut Christus justitia nostra nominatur. Ita nempe vocatur Christus, ut significetur, nihil esse internum & inhaerens in nobis, cuius vi & virtute coram Dei tribunali consistere, aut absolutionem & remissionem peccatorum impetrare valeamus: itaque extra nos esse totum illud, quod est nostrae justificationis meritorium, justitia nimirum quae Christi est propria, nostra non est nisi imputatione. Atqui tale aliquid de Adamo dici non potest. Nam praeterquam quod Adami peccatum actuale meritorium est poenarum, quae nobis incumbunt; est etiam internum aliquid & in nobis inhaerens, cuius merito etiam condemnationi subjacemus, nimirum nativa nostra corruptio, quae una cum imputato Adae peccato facit unum veluti corpus reatus, quo Deus judicio suo nos tenet obnoxios. En igitur causa esse potest, quare non dixerit Scriptura Adamum esse peccatum nostrum, sicut dixit Christum esse justitiam nostram.
latin.321: PLAC. Agnoscit ergo vir doctus non eodem prorsus modo per Adami inobedientiam nos coram tribunali Dei constitui peccatores, quo per Christi obedientiam constituimur justi: itaque non esse urgandam illam similitudinem, quasi nullum esset in modo discrimen: hoc vero est totum, quod hac interrogatione, siquidem ea sumus usi, probare instituimus. Quare pro nobis, non contra nos haec eius militat responsio. Videntur tamen in ea quaedam digna reprehensione. Illud in primis, quod ait, justitiam Christi nostram non esse nisi imputatione: nam si similiter, ut passim contendit, peccatum Adami nostrum non est nisi imputatione, eodem modo ambo nostra sunt, nec ea in re ullum est discrimen. Id quod pugnat cum Apostolo, maximum in modo, quo nostra sunt, justitia Christi & iniustitia Adami, discrimen innuente, cum illam appellat donum, & gratiam, & donationem quae est ex gratia: sic enim modum significat quo fit nostra: quo modo nostrum nec factum est, nec fieri potuit Adami peccatum.
latin.322: Deinde quorsum observat hoc loco, justitiam Christi propriam, non esse nostram nisi imputatione, si idem censet de peccato quod Adami est proprium, id similiter non esse nostrum nisi imputatione? Quid enim hoc facit ad discrimen inter Christum & Adamum explicandum? Quod si id non censet, sibi ipse contradicit, quippe qui id aliquoties inculcavit. Praeterea, si est aliquid in nobis internum & inhaerens cujus merito condemnationi subjacemus, cur eo merito eaque condemnatione non contenti, volumus aliud peccatum extra nos positum immediate imputari? Nempe, inquies, ut sit hujus interni causa, quo alioqui careremus. Delectatur igitur Deus hoc interno peccato, quippe qui sine ulla necessitate libere nobis illud extra nos positum peccatum imputat, ut vi illius imputationis producatur internum illud in nobis peccatum, quod alioqui non posset produci. Hoccine est glorificare Deum, & non potius eum facere, (quod sine horrore conscientiae pronunciare non possum,) autorem peccati nostri?
latin.323: Denique, quomodo imputatum illud peccatum & corruptio nativa faciunt unum veluti corpus reatus, si haec illius est poena proprie dicta? Antecedit enim reatus poenam; & qui adeo reos facit imputatum peccatum, ut simus illa corruptione & morte aeterna digni, eius reatus non dimidiatus videtur reatus, sed perfectus & integer. Quod si unum componunt corpus reatus, vel eum reatum integrum intellexit Apostolus Rom. 5. atque ita alio modo condemnamur per Adamum, quam justificamur per Christum, quod passim negat vir doctus, vel intellexit dimidiam tantum illius reatus partem, id quod, opinor, nemo dixerit. Ultimam quaestionem visum est differre in suum, qui mox occurret, proprium locum. Pergis quaerendo; Quae enim, inquis, ratio assignari potest, cur parvuli, qui nondum peccarunt actualiter, moriantur, vel in utero matrum, vel nascendo, vel statim post nativitatem, nisi haec, quod peccatum Adami, per quod mors pervasit in omnes homines, illis imputetur? Ego contra quaero, qua ratio assignari possit, cur parvulis peccatum actuale Adami, tanto antequam esse inciperent admissum, nondum usum rationis assecutis imputetur ad mortem? Interim tuae quaestioni satisfacio: assigno rationem, vitium illis inhaerens a conceptione. Testem laudo Confessionem Fidei Art. XI.

pass_a.318: Placeus presses that 'is said' in the erotema is not aimed at Scripture alone, as the Learned Man takes it, but at Scripture together with all the theologians, who never called Adam our sin, or our unrighteousness, or us unrighteousness in Adam. The diversity of phrases when Christ and Adam are handled in justification and condemnation already argues diversity and disparity between them. We are gladly content with the phrases Scripture uses—yet we ought still to weigh carefully why God expressed His mind thus or thus, or left it unspoken; the Apostles went before us in that, sometimes even urging Scripture's silence. And in the Apostle there are no locutions that manifestly mark immediate imputation—none even obscurely.
pass_a.319: GAR's second reply: places calling Christ our righteousness never compare Adam and Christ; had Paul compared them as in Romans 5, he might have called Adam our sin as Christ is our righteousness, even if not on altogether the same account. Placeus reverses the point: where the Apostle institutes no Christ/Adam comparison he uses that Christ-locution, and where he does compare them he abstains from it. Respect is also owed to all the theologians, who never apply that locution to Adam.
pass_a.320: GAR's third offers a probable reason: Christ is called our righteousness to show nothing internal and inherent in us can stand us before God's tribunal or win remission—so all justifying merit is outside us, Christ's own righteousness, ours only by imputation. No such thing can be said of Adam. Besides his actual sin meriting the penalties that lie on us, there is also native corruption inherent in us by whose desert we lie under condemnation; together with Adam's imputed sin it forms as it were one body of guilt by which God holds us liable. That, GAR says, is why Scripture never said 'Adam our sin' as it said 'Christ our righteousness.'
pass_a.321: Placeus: GAR has now conceded the modes differ—Adam's disobedience does not constitute us sinners before the tribunal in just the same way Christ's obedience constitutes us righteous—so the likeness must not be pressed as if mode were identical; that was the whole point of the question, and the reply helps Placeus, not against him. But some things deserve censure. First, saying Christ's righteousness is ours only by imputation, while also holding Adam's sin ours only by imputation, erases mode-difference in that point and clashes with the Apostle, who hints a great difference by calling Christ's side gift, grace, and a donation of grace—the mode by which it becomes ours, a mode Adam's sin never had and could not have.
pass_a.322: Next: if GAR holds Adam's own sin likewise ours only by imputation, how does that explain Christ/Adam difference—and if not, he contradicts what he has driven home several times. Further, if something inherent already deserts condemnation, why, not content with that desert, demand another sin placed outside us immediately imputed? You will say: to cause that internal vice we would otherwise lack. Then God freely, without necessity, imputes an outside sin so that by its force inner sin is produced—delighting in that internal evil. Is that to glorify God, or rather to make Him (spoken with horror of conscience) author of our sin?
pass_a.323: Finally Placeus asks how imputed sin and native corruption make as it were one body of guilt if the corruption is properly the penalty of that imputed sin. Guilt precedes penalty; and an imputed sin that already makes us worthy of that corruption and eternal death looks like perfect whole guilt, not a halved remnant. If they compose one body of guilt, either the Apostle in Romans 5 understood that whole—and then we are condemned through Adam in another mode than we are justified through Christ, which the Learned Man everywhere denies—or he understood only half that guilt's part, which Placeus thinks no one has said. He defers the last erotema to its own soon place, then meets the infant-death question head-on: not Adam's actual sin, committed ages before they began to be, charged unto death to babes without use of reason, but the vice inherent in them from conception. He cites as witness the Confession of Faith, Article XI. Tip before deeper Pighius/infant clash.

318: But the word 'is said' in this interrogation is not to be taken relative to Scripture alone, as the learned man does, but relative to Scripture and all the theologians, who never said Adam is our sin, or our unrighteousness, or that we are unrighteousness in Adam. For the diversity of phrases when Christ and Adam are treated in the matter of justification and condemnation argues diversity and disparity between the two. And so it becomes us to be content with those phrases which occur in Scripture—and truly we are greatly content with them—yet it also becomes us to consider those phrases attentively, and to weigh the reasons why God thus or thus expressed His mind, or did not express it; in which the Apostles went before us by their example, sometimes even urging Scripture's very silence. But there are no locutions in the Apostle which manifestly mark immediate imputation; indeed none have been seen that mark it even obscurely.
319: GAR. 2. In those places where Christ is called our righteousness, no comparison is instituted between Adam and Christ: which if it had been instituted, as was done in Romans 5, who does not know whether Paul would have used that phrase by which he would teach that Adam is our sin, as Christ is our righteousness, even if not altogether on the same account. PLAC. But I argue from this: that where the Apostle institutes no comparison between Christ and Adam he uses that locution of Christ, but where he institutes some comparison between the two he abstains from it. Although, as I said, respect is had not to Scripture alone but also to all the theologians, who never use that locution of Adam.
320: GAR. 3. Yet a probable reason can be given why Adam is not called our sin as Christ is named our righteousness. For Christ is so called that it may be signified there is nothing internal and inherent in us by whose force and virtue we can stand before God's tribunal, or obtain absolution and remission of sins: and so all that is meritorious of our justification is outside us—namely the righteousness which is Christ's own, ours only by imputation. But no such thing can be said of Adam. For besides that Adam's actual sin is meritorious of the penalties that lie on us, there is also something internal and inherent in us by whose desert we also lie under condemnation—namely our native corruption, which together with Adam's imputed sin makes as it were one body of guilt by which God in His judgment holds us liable. See then a cause why Scripture did not say Adam is our sin as it said Christ is our righteousness.
321: PLAC. The learned man therefore acknowledges that we are not constituted sinners before God's tribunal by Adam's disobedience in altogether the same mode in which we are constituted righteous by Christ's obedience: and so that likeness is not to be pressed as if there were no difference in the mode: and this is the whole of what we meant to prove by this interrogation, if indeed we used it. Therefore his reply fights for us, not against us. Yet some things in it seem worthy of censure. First, that he says Christ's righteousness is ours only by imputation: for if likewise, as he everywhere contends, Adam's sin is ours only by imputation, both are ours in the same mode, and there is no difference in that point. That clashes with the Apostle, who hints a very great difference in the mode by which Christ's righteousness and Adam's unrighteousness are ours, when he calls the former a gift, and grace, and a donation which is of grace: for so he signifies the mode by which it becomes ours—a mode in which Adam's sin neither was made ours, nor could be.
322: Next, to what end does he observe here that Christ's own righteousness is ours only by imputation, if he holds the same of the sin that is Adam's own—that it likewise is ours only by imputation? What does that do to explain the difference between Christ and Adam? Or if he does not hold that, he contradicts himself, seeing he has driven it home several times. Further, if there is something internal and inherent in us by whose desert we lie under condemnation, why, not content with that desert and that condemnation, do we want another sin placed outside us to be immediately imputed? You will say: that it may be the cause of this internal thing, which otherwise we would lack. God then delights in this internal sin, seeing that without any necessity He freely imputes to us that sin placed outside us, so that by the force of that imputation that internal sin may be produced in us which otherwise could not be produced. Is this to glorify God, and not rather to make Him (which I cannot pronounce without horror of conscience) the author of our sin?
323: Finally, how do that imputed sin and native corruption make as it were one body of guilt, if the latter is properly the penalty of the former? For guilt precedes penalty; and the imputed sin that so makes us guilty that we are worthy of that corruption and eternal death—its guilt does not seem a halved guilt, but perfect and whole. And if they compose one body of guilt, either the Apostle in Romans 5 understood that whole guilt—and so we are condemned through Adam in another mode than we are justified through Christ, which the learned man everywhere denies—or he understood only half that guilt's part, which I think no one has said. The last question it seemed good to defer to its own place, which will soon occur. You go on asking: What reason, you say, can be assigned why little ones who have not yet sinned actually should die, whether in their mothers' womb, or in being born, or right after birth, unless this—that Adam's sin, through which death pervaded all men, is imputed to them? I ask on the contrary: what reason can be assigned why Adam's actual sin, committed so long before they began to be, should be imputed unto death to little ones who have not yet attained the use of reason? Meanwhile I satisfy your question: I assign the reason—the vice inherent in them from conception. I call as witness the Confession of Faith, Article XI.
